story.title: BO Team Exploits Log4Shell in VMware vCenter, Compromises Russian Firm's Code-Signing Server
story.text: An investigation into suspicious activity within a Russian software developer's network has uncovered a months-long compromise of its development infrastructure and a software code-signing server. The activity, documented by Kaspersky's ICS CERT team after it was contacted by the affected developer in June 2025, has been attributed to a threat actor named BO Team (aka Black Owl, Hoody Hyena, and Lifting Zmiy). The name of the targeted company was not disclosed, but it operates from within Russia and develops software that has a "customer base in the Russian Federation," according to Kaspersky. Over the course of several months, the intrusion resulted in the theft of confidential information and the compromise of all components of the organization's IT infrastructure, including Windows and Linux servers, workstations, hypervisors, backup servers, security solution management servers, and network equipment. Active since at least 2023, BO Team focuses on cyber espionage and hacktivism, and has a history of targeting Russian entities to steal valuable data and break into compromised infrastructure using tools like Mythic and Cobalt Strike, along with its own malware such as BrockenDoor and ZeronetKit. The group is assessed to be of Ukrainian origin. "Their primary motivation is to degrade the Russian military-industrial complex to weaken Moscow's operational capabilities on the battlefield," Orange Cyberdefense said in an analysis of the group. "They also engage in cognitive warfare aimed at humiliating Russian institutions and demonstrating their vulnerability to Ukrainian digital resistance." While BO Team is known to deploy ransomware and publicize its activities on a dedicated Telegram channel, the attack targeting the unspecified software developer did not involve any data destruction or public posts claiming responsibility for it. "Instead, the attackers worked to entrench themselves in the victim's network by setting up convenient command channels and planting backdoors to restore access in case it was lost," Kaspersky said. "The compromise of the software development (CI/CD) infrastructure and the software code-signing server indicated that the attack would likely develop into a supply chain scenario." The attack, per the Russian cybersecurity company, involved the threat actors compromising the organization's Linux terminal server by taking advantage of an exposed SSH service, and using it to conduct reconnaissance of the internal network to flag systems with accessible SMB, Kerberos, SSH, Telnet, FTP, HTTP, HTTPS, WinRM, and LDAP services. The adversary has also been found unsuccessfully attempting to access internal portals, along with websites like proxy-sale[.]com, start.duckduckgo[.]com, vcsa.vmware[.]com, and vulners[.]com, among others. Event logs show that the attackers further attempted to connect from the compromised terminal server to the virtualization system servers, including logging in to the VMware vCenter web interface. These sign-in efforts ended in failure. However, the threat actor managed to successfully target a VMware vCenter server (version 7.0.3) vulnerable to CVE-2021-44228 (aka Log4Shell and LogJam), obtain a remote command line with root privileges, connect to the hypervisor over SSH, and identify accessible hosts. This phase also involved the deployment of a backdoor on the hypervisor that was run every hour by planting a shell script in the "/etc/cron.hourly/" directory. The script carried the name "pgcache" in a likely attempt to disguise it as a legitimate PostgreSQL component. The primary responsibility of the backdoor is to download and run a secondary shell script from "lo1yaizaeghaevarooD1ahtaichootae.nofrillsdns[.]com." The shell script is designed to download and run the Global Socket (GSocket) utility, enabling the attacker to gain remote control of the compromised host. Select variants of the script have been found to point to a hostname-specific payload staged on "lo1yaizaeghaevarood1ahtaichootaz.nofrillsdns[.]com" to deliver an as-yet-undetermined next-stage payload. "The attackers used the nofrillsdns[.]com service, which allows domain names to be created for free by calling the curl utility," Kaspersky said. "By default, when the malware's command-and-control server is not operating, the attackers set the corresponding DNS record to 127.0.0.1, which is what the script checks. Activating the backdoor requires only a change to the DNS record -- the script will then download and run the malware." Some of the other post-exploitation actions undertaken by the BO Team following the backdoor deployment are listed below - - Gaining access to the corporate proxy server. - Abusing the certificate of the compromised hypervisor to connect to servers associated with a second virtualization cluster and place a similar backdoor. - Collecting information about virtual machines and firewall rules, accessing some of them via a command-line interpreter in the guest OS from the hypervisor. - Running an obfuscated bash script to decrypt and run an ELF binary designed to provide remote control over SSH. - Searching for secrets on the compromised virtual machines, allowing the attackers to breach the virtual machine of the GitLab software development platform, as well as gain access to some of the repositories containing source code and seize the server's private key. - Using the private key of the GitLab virtual machine to connect to the organization's Ansible orchestration system. - Using access to the Linux terminal server to locate credentials of several domain accounts and connect to the domain controller using the account of one of the system administrators after likely accessing the memory of virtual machines running on the compromised hypervisors. - Changing the security attributes of the user's Windows Downloads directory. - Using legitimate binaries like tasklist.exe, findstr.exe, taskmgr.exe, and ipconfig.exe to identify which security solutions were running on the system and to gather details about network interfaces. - Attempting to take a dump of the lsass.exe process using the Nanodump utility and obtain the credentials of domain administrators and other privileged users with access to the domain controller. The attackers deleted the event logs after the activity was detected and blocked by a security solution. - Using system utilities such as comsvcs.dll rather than established utilities like Mimikatz and Nanodump to create a memory dump of the lsass.exe process. - Dumping the system registry using the regedit.exe utility, and using it to decrypt the Active Directory domain database ("ntds.dit") to extract the credentials of all domain users. - Launching the OpenSSH scp.exe utility to transfer the collected information to the terminal server. - Logging in to the domain controller using the Kerberos ticket of one of the domain administrators and ultimately compromising the organization's entire Windows infrastructure by taking advantage of the fact that the same password was used for system administrator accounts in different domains. - Connecting to the terminal server over SSH using root account credentials after possibly stealing them from a system administrator's computer post obtaining domain administrator privileges. - Modifying "/usr/bin/nxnode-login" to intercept and write user credentials to a shared-memory file at "/dev/shm/pulse-shm-3088612174." - Successfully brute-forcing the password of the administrator's terminal server after about 2,500 failed attempts to place the private key of the Ansible system. - Complicating detection efforts by timestomping, obfuscation of malware code, usage of living-off-the-land (LotL) techniques, systematic deletion of event logs, and dressing up malware files as legitimate software. "We found numerous traces of BO Team connecting to various Windows servers, though the attackers only used malware in one case," Kaspersky explained. "The server which apparently held particular interest for hackers, was used to sign compiled builds of the commercial software developed by the attacked organization." "Attackers may be interested in such a server for two reasons. First, they may try to carry out a supply chain attack by injecting malicious code into a product build right before it is signed. Second, the attackers may try to steal the organization's digital signature to use later to sign malware." It's suspected that the attackers likely attempted to execute a malicious WMI script and install a backdoor similar to the Linux variant in the temporary files directory. But after the incident was detected and countermeasures were enacted, the attackers, after having lost access to the compromised infrastructure, orchestrated a phishing campaign towards the end of July in an attempt to collect employee credentials. The phishing email contained the "Account disconnected from the mail server" subject line and sought to trick the recipient into clicking on a link to change their password. What's more, the email managed to bypass SPF and DKIM checks, indicating the attackers had in their possession a private key that was obtained after gaining control of the organization's mail server. The phishing attack was detected and prevented. "The attackers used a service that automatically generates phishing pages," Kaspersky said. "The service loads the content of a targeted organization's official website and displays a password entry form on top of the official site's layout. After entering the password, the user sees an error message. However, the information is actually sent to the attacker." "We repeatedly noted that the attackers tried not to use malware and hacking utilities in order to evade detection," Kaspersky said. "Instead, they actively used system tools such as RDP, SSH, and SCP, as well as system utilities to steal user credentials. This enabled them to develop the attack using legitimate accounts, which also matches the BO Team prof

content.what_happened: BO Team exploited a Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228) on a VMware vCenter server (version 7.0.3) to gain root access, then deployed a cron-based backdoor that downloaded and executed a remote-control utility via a nofrillsdns domain, ultimately compromising the entire IT infrastructure of a Russian software developer.
content.who_affected: A Russian software development company (name not disclosed) with a customer base in the Russian Federation, whose Linux terminal server, hypervisors, GitLab platform, Ansible system, and Windows domain were all infiltrated.
content.what_changed: The attackers moved from initial SSH access on a terminal server to full infrastructure domination, including code-signing server compromise, credential theft from domain controllers, and placement of persistent backdoors across hypervisors, CI/CD pipelines, and orchestration systems.
content.mitigation: The article does not describe a fix or remediation step taken by the victim or vendor.

history.title: New NoisyTCP vulnerability lets attackers crash Linux servers
history.text: An 11-year-old Linux kernel vulnerability, dubbed NoisyTCP, affects almost all Linux distributions and lets attackers crash systems running Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers with default configurations. According to Hyunwoo Kim, the security researcher who discovered it, this pre-authenticated remote corruption flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-99288) stems from a NULL pointer dereference weakness in the Linux kernel's TCP networking subsystem. Unauthenticated attackers can trigger it remotely via maliciously crafted TCP packets that exploit the timing between SYN cookie handling and socket hashing to crash the kernel and operating system on targeted servers. However, while CVE-2026-99288 exploits cause a kernel panic and take down the host, they don't allow threat actors to alter data or gain arbitrary code execution. Kim added that although attackers can exploit this vulnerability against any Linux system that receives TCP packets directly and runs Nginx, Apache, or an SSH server, "the race window is narrow, so triggering it against a quiet bare-metal server can take a long time." "Due to a race condition during lockless socket lookups, recycled socket memory can be accessed before it is properly initialized and hashed. A remote attacker could exploit this issue by generating network traffic that drives socket reuse, triggering a NULL pointer dereference and kernel crash that results in a Denial of Service (DoS)," the Red Hat security team explained. "To trigger this vulnerability, a stale ehash lookup and the freeing and reallocation of an existing request socket must proceed concurrently in different RX contexts. Packet processing has to be spread out by using the difference in receive hash between IPv4 fragments and regular TCP packets, so it can be triggered against servers that have two or more RX queues, or where RPS distributes packets across multiple CPUs," the researcher said. While a CVE-2026-99288 patch is already available and a fix was already merged into the mainline Linux kernel two weeks ago, the researcher advised those who can't apply it or upgrade immediately to disable SYN cookies (which will unfortunately lower protection against SYN flood attacks) and serialize to a single RX queue to block the race required for successful exploitation. In May, Kim also disclosed Dirty Frag, a Linux local privilege escalation flaw that chains RxRPC (CVE-2026-43500) and xfrm-ESP (CVE-2026-43284) page-cache write flaws to gain root access on major distributions, including Ubuntu, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, CentOS Stream, and Fedora. More recently, in July, he also disclosed Januscape, a 16-year-old Linux kernel vulnerability that enables attackers to escape a virtual machine and run arbitrary code on the host. history.summary: A newly disclosed 11-year-old Linux kernel vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288, allows unauthenticated remote attackers to crash systems running Nginx, Apache, or SSH servers with default configurations. The flaw stems from a NULL pointer dereference in the TCP networking subsystem, triggered by exploiting timing between SYN cookie handling and socket hashing. Successful exploitation causes a kernel panic and Denial of Service, but does not enable data alteration or arbitrary code execution.

history.title: Microsoft Rules Out Cyberattack in Outage, Warns of Phishing Campaign
history.text: Microsoft says its recent Microsoft 365 outage was not caused by a cyberattack, but warns that attackers used the disruption to send phishing emails disguised as service notifications. The November 12 outage disrupted access to Exchange Online mailboxes and Outlook. The tech giant also identified possible effects on services such as Teams, SharePoint Online and Microsoft 365 Copilot. Organizations and government agencies in several countries reported interruptions to email and other operations. “This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents,” Microsoft said in a statement on Friday. The company traced the failure to an earlier network capacity upgrade, with a subsequent network change exposing the problem. Microsoft said it fixed the underlying issue and was bringing services back in stages to ensure they remained stable. The Exchange Online incident, tracked as EX1550543, was marked resolved on November 13. Microsoft Threat Intelligence said it observed a phishing campaign exploiting the disruption. The fake emails posed as Microsoft 365 service health notices and referred to EX1550543, the actual incident identifier. In some messages detected on November 13, recipients were falsely told that emails held during the outage would be deleted within 24 hours unless they clicked a link to restore them. The phishing emails’ subject lines began with “Outage -” followed by a six-character code. Sender display names included organization-specific wording followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.” Microsoft identified three domains used to send the emails: moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com. Recipient-specific SendGrid tracking links redirected to reallifeaccounting[.]com. Similar messages targeted organizations across several US sectors. “The activity is consistent with credential phishing, although credential collection and malware delivery have not been confirmed,” Microsoft said. The company subsequently reported that its security products were blocking the campaign. Microsoft recommended that security teams examine suspicious emails and links, investigate user clicks, and review their Safe Links policies. It also advised organizations to verify service incidents directly through the Microsoft 365 admin center. Related: No Signs of Hacking in FAA Ground Stop as FBI Reportedly Probes Software Update Related: Microsoft Struggles to Restore Email and Other Services in a Global Outage Related: Ahold Delhaize Restoring Services Disrupted by Cyberattack
history.summary: Microsoft stated that the November 12 Microsoft 365 outage was caused by a technical issue stemming from a network capacity upgrade and subsequent network change, not a cyberattack. Attackers exploited the disruption by sending phishing emails disguised as service health notifications, referencing the incident ID EX1550543 and using subject lines starting with "Outage-" followed by a six-character code. Microsoft fixed the underlying issue and restored services in stages, while its security products blocked the associated phishing campaign.

history.title: FBI warns ARTEX AI hacking tool is powering global cyberattacks
history.text: The FBI is warning that hackers are using an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX to automate cyberattacks against organizations worldwide, including a recent ConnectWise supply-chain breach that compromised Microsoft 365 customer environments. In a FLASH advisory released Friday, the agency said multiple threat actors have weaponized the open-source framework since at least August 2026 to target organizations across the financial, government, technology, defense, healthcare, and other sectors. "ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours," reads the FBI advisory. "The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale." ARTEX is an autonomous penetration testing framework written in Go that uses artificial intelligence agents to perform reconnaissance, discover vulnerabilities, exploit systems, escalate privileges, and steal data with little human intervention. Rather than using its own AI model, the framework integrates with external large language models (LLMs), including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, GLM, Grok, and Kimi. Attackers provide their goals and tasks to ARTEX, which converts them into commands executed by specialized AI agents. This allows them to automate intrusion activities and target multiple organizations simultaneously. The FBI says the framework is particularly effective at identifying vulnerabilities in overlooked systems, including partner portals, employee applications, legacy services, and third-party integrations. While these automated attacks can generate large volumes of suspicious traffic that trigger security alerts, their speed can leave defenders with little time to respond before attackers breach a system. ARTEX was originally released on GitHub in July 2026 by a developer known as Autumn-27, who removed the repository on October 8 after reports emerged that threat actors were abusing the framework. However, the FBI says the framework remains available through community forks, archived copies, localized versions, and a commercial edition called ARTEX PRO. As of early November, researchers had identified more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles, with the actual number of deployments believed to be significantly higher. The FBI's 13-page advisory includes indicators of compromise associated with known ARTEX campaigns, including IP addresses, command-and-control infrastructure, and suspicious network activity. Separately, cybersecurity researcher MalwareMustDie released an open-source ARTEX detection signature pack on Friday to help defenders identify attacks involving the framework. The detection pack includes rules and indicators for various security monitoring and threat detection tools, covering suspicious network requests, identity abuse, cloud activity, malicious files, and automated attack patterns. The researcher also published a detection playbook that categorizes indicators by confidence level, warning that IP addresses and other infrastructure indicators can become outdated or generate false positives. Organizations are urged to secure internet-facing applications, restrict access to cloud administration interfaces, review application permissions and authentication logs, and implement rate limits on sensitive APIs. The bureau also recommends monitoring for unusual bursts of automated requests, suspicious cloud activity, unexpected credential or privilege changes, and large data transfers. The FBI cautions that IP addresses listed in the IOCs may have changed since the attacks occurred. Organizations that identify suspicious activity associated with ARTEX are encouraged to report their findings to the FBI or its Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3). Known Artex-linked attacks The advisory highlights several previously reported cyberattacks involving ARTEX, including the October ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain attack that allowed hackers to gain unauthorized access to Microsoft 365 customer environments. The attack compromised application identities used by ConnectWise's cloud backup service, formerly known as SkyKick Cloud Backup, allowing attackers to authenticate to customer tenants using permissions previously granted to the applications. At the time, cybersecurity firm Huntress reported identifying at least 162 compromised tenants. In an investigation published in October, Microsoft attributed the campaign to a China-state-aligned threat actor tracked as Storm-0940, which used ARTEX to accelerate reconnaissance, password spraying, and abuse of cloud application permissions. After compromising ConnectWise application identities, the attackers used ARTEX to attempt authentication against more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 tenants, with some intrusions progressing to credential modifications and attempts to establish persistent access. The FBI also referenced attacks against South Korean financial institutions that exposed personal information belonging to approximately 67,000 people. In that campaign, a Chinese-speaking threat actor combined ARTEX with Claude Code agents to attack multiple banks, including Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank, and Hana Bank. Researchers at CrowdStrike discovered the attacker's exposed infrastructure, which contained ARTEX configuration files, Claude Code session histories, and other records documenting the intrusions. In a separate investigation, South Korean police arrested seven suspects linked to attacks against more than 90 organizations, with ARTEX reportedly used in most of the intrusions. Authorities said the gang stole approximately 8.2 million data records from organizations including hospitals, educational institutions, and businesses. More recently, CrowdStrike reported that a Chinese cyberespionage group tracked as Vapor Panda used ARTEX in automated attacks targeting more than 200 organizations across 14 countries. The campaign compromised at least nine organizations, with AI agents performing reconnaissance, exploiting vulnerabilities, deploying web shells, stealing credentials, and pursuing different attack paths when initial attempts failed. history.summary: FBI warns that the AI-powered penetration testing framework ARTEX is being used by hackers to automate global cyberattacks, enabling intrusions from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours with minimal technical expertise. The framework, originally released on GitHub in July 2026 and later removed but still available via forks and a commercial edition, integrates with external large language models and has been linked to supply-chain breaches, financial institution attacks, and espionage campaigns targeting hundreds of organizations worldwide. The FBI and security researchers have shared indicators of compromise and detection signatures to help identify ARTEX activity, while urging organizations to secure internet-facing applications, restrict cloud administration access, enforce rate limits, and monitor for automated requests and suspicious credential changes.

history.title: TSMC employee data breach linked to cloud provider
history.text: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) confirmed that personal employee data has been leaked online after a threat actor put 6.9GB of information allegedly stolen from the company up for auction. The technology giant said the incident affected current and former employees but doesn’t impact its operations or customers. The company verified the leaked information and confirmed that it matched "data stored in the system services of a cloud service provider," indicating an external breach. TSMC is the world’s largest contract chipmaker, manufacturing advanced processors and other semiconductors for companies such as Apple and Nvidia. Last year, it shipped approximately 15 million 12-inch-equivalent wafers and generated $122.4 billion in annual revenue. TSMC's investigation found that the leaked information matched data stored in a cloud service provider it uses, pointing to a breach outside its own infrastructure. The company is now notifying impacted staff and providing the necessary support, while also engaging a third-party cybersecurity firm to help manage the situation. “TSMC has found that some of our current and former employee data was made available on an external website without authorization,” TSMC says in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). “Currently, we have found no evidence that TSMC’s systems have been compromised,” the company added. Threat actor auctions the data On November 8, someone using the alias ‘SmithBianl’ leaked on a hacker forum a text file containing 499 rows of information allegedly stolen from TSMC. The actor claimed the file was a sample of a 6.9GB dataset containing 46,000 employee records. According to the post, the leaked information included TSMC employees' national ID numbers, addresses, contact details, and banking information. SmithBianl offered the data for auction, with bidding starting at 3 BTC (approximately $65,000). In the absence of a buyer, they warned that the data would be leaked for free in one week, setting the first deadline to November 15. BleepingComputer has contacted TSMC to ask whether they have engaged with the threat actor and whether they planned to pay the hackers to prevent a full public leak of their employees’ data. A spokesperson declined to comment at this stage. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. history.summary: TSMC confirmed that personal employee data was leaked online after a threat actor posted 6.9GB of information allegedly stolen from the company, affecting current and former employees but not operations or customers. The breach originated from data stored in the system services of a cloud service provider that TSMC uses, not from TSMC's own infrastructure. TSMC stated there is no evidence its systems were compromised, and it is notifying impacted staff while engaging a third-party cybersecurity firm to manage the situation. Fix: TSMC is notifying affected employees and working with a third-party cybersecurity firm to investigate and mitigate the breach.

history.title: Pentagon Renames CDAO ‘Super Intelligence Office’
history.text: The Pentagon on Friday renamed its Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO) the Super Intelligence Office, adopting the terminology President Donald Trump has directed federal agencies to use instead of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Cameron Stanley continues to lead the office as Chief Super Intelligence Officer for the Department of War (DoW), with Andrew Mapes serving as Principal Deputy Super Intelligence Officer. Stanley took over as the Pentagon’s chief digital and AI officer in January after leading national security transformation at Amazon Web Services. He previously led Project Maven, the Pentagon’s military AI initiative. The Department of War moved the office’s public resources, procurement information and partnership portals to SI.mil domain and said existing programs, solicitations and defense partnerships would continue without interruption. The office’s portfolio includes the Maven Smart System, an AI-enabled intelligence and targeting platform, and the War Data Platform, a central hub for military data. “This redesignation is a clear signal of where the Department of War is going,” said Stanley. “We have moved beyond experimental prototypes. As the Super Intelligence Office our mission is to harness the full power of sovereign Super Intelligence to ensure decisive military superiority across every domain.” The rebrand follows Trump’s executive order (14434) in September directing agencies to use “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in official communications and other non-statutory documents, to the maximum extent permitted by law. In October, Trump announced the “Super Intelligence Force,” a government-wide AI coordination group chaired by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. The Justice Department announced its own Super Intelligence Task Force on November 5 to coordinate civil and criminal enforcement involving AI, including cases of fraud and unlawful uses targeting critical infrastructure. Related: Is AI Making Us Worse at Cybersecurity? Related: The Key to AI Software Security Isn’t Speed, It’s Maturity
history.summary: The Pentagon renamed its Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office to the Super Intelligence Office, aligning with President Trump's directive for federal agencies to use "Super Intelligence" terminology instead of AI. Cameron Stanley continues as Chief Super Intelligence Officer, overseeing the office's portfolio which includes the Maven Smart System and War Data Platform, with resources moved to the SI.mil domain. The rebrand follows executive order 14434 and coincides with the establishment of a government-wide Super Intelligence Force and a new Justice Department task force focused on AI-related enforcement.

history.title: Italy Fines Meta €805 Million Over Facebook's Android Gallery Access Without Explicit Consent
history.text: Meta was fined €805 million in Italy yesterday over a Facebook for Android feature that suggests photos and videos from users' phone galleries for them to post. The Garante, Italy's data protection authority, found that the feature was enabled by default and that the app accessed Italian users' photos, videos, and related metadata without their explicit consent. The company has 60 days to switch the feature off by default, including for people who have already granted the app gallery access, and to request consent separately. Meta plans to appeal and calls the fine "disproportionate", a spokesperson said in a statement reported by Reuters. The app asks for gallery access via a single permission that covers the whole app and several functions with different purposes, the authority found. A general notice about enabling other features appears first, but it does not make it clear to users that they are also enabling gallery suggestions. Fully granted, a permission like this lets the app read the phone's whole photo archive, usually on an ongoing basis. Neither the user nor the authority can check which information is actually used. The authority found a breach of Article 122 of Italy's Privacy Code, which puts the EU's ePrivacy Directive into Italian law. That rule treats a phone as part of a person's private life. Any access to what the phone stores, therefore, requires free and informed consent, whether or not data is sent anywhere or harm results. The authority's order, set out in its press release, requires the company to: - Within 60 days, ask for consent through a separate, specific request for this feature, and explain clearly what the feature is for, that it accesses the gallery, and how to turn it off. - Within 60 days, keep the feature off by default, including for people who already granted the permission. - Within 30 days, report to the authority on the work it has started, and within 90 days, on the measures it has taken. If the company misses the 60-day deadline, the feature cannot be switched on for anyone who has not given valid consent. Meta said in a statement quoted in a Reuters report that the feature works only after users give permission on their device, and that they can change that permission at any time in their settings. The Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti, the Bolzano consumer protection group whose complaint started the investigation, published consumer advice on July 11, 2025. It told users to switch off the gallery suggestion settings in the app and to check what access and permissions the Facebook app has on their phone. The investigation did not look at whether gallery content was used to train AI models. The company denies any such use. The authority may separately examine a newer feature, launched this year, that allows gallery content to be processed in the cloud. The company had argued that Ireland's data protection authority should handle the case. The Garante rejected that argument because the ePrivacy rules do not provide a one-stop-shop mechanism. The feature has been available since 2023. The investigation began in July 2025 and included the authority's own technical analysis. The fine equals about 0.47% of the group's global revenue. In setting it, the authority weighed the large number of people involved, about 20 million Android users in Italy. It also weighed how long the breach has lasted. The breach is still ongoing for people who have not updated the app, and for those who have already granted permission, the authority said. Other factors were a 2019 decision against the company and limited cooperation during the investigation. Changes the company made after the complaint counted in its favor, though the authority judged them late and limited to people who update the app.
history.summary: Italy's data protection authority fined Meta €805 million for enabling Facebook's Android gallery suggestion feature by default without users' explicit consent. The Garante found the app accessed Italian users' photos, videos, and metadata through a broad permission that didn't clearly inform users about gallery suggestions, breaching Article 122 of Italy's Privacy Code. Meta has 60 days to switch the feature off by default and request separate consent, or the feature cannot be turned on for anyone without valid consent. Fix: Meta must switch the gallery suggestion feature off by default within 60 days and request separate, specific consent from users, explaining what the feature does and how to disable it.

history.title: Tor Updates DoS Defenses Again as Relay Attacks Continue
history.text: The Tor Project has released new security fixes for its core software as a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack continues to strain the volunteer-run relays that make up its network. Tor 0.4.9.17, announced on November 13, patches several security issues. The project singled out one fix related to how relays’ built-in DoS protections deal with IPv6. “This release comes in rapid response to the ongoing DDoS attack on the network, which has affected most relay operators. This is not an easy problem to address, as relays across the network are being overwhelmed by a massive flood of client circuits,” Tor developer David Goulet said in the announcement. According to the project, more defenses are under consideration, and new versions should follow shortly. Anyone running a relay has been urged to update without delay. The latest version comes less than three weeks after Tor 0.4.9.15, which introduced three DoS protections against what the project described as a “thunderstorm” of directory requests. Writing to relay operators at the time, Goulet noted that a single relay could be hit with hundreds of circuits per second. He cautioned that relays would remain under heavy load for as long as the attack lasted. Reports from relay operators suggest the latest update hasn’t ended the disruption. In a forum post on November 14, one operator said two of their relays had lost HSDir status due to attacks before the update, and that another was being targeted when 0.4.9.17 was released and installed. Roughly ten minutes after that relay was upgraded, the attack took on a new form, according to the operator. Its traffic plunged and it kept becoming unresponsive. “Relay unresponsiveness ultimately caused loss of HSDIR. Attack ceased immediately on loss of HSDIR,” the operator wrote. In the operator’s view, 0.4.9.17 does not do enough to shield HSDir relays, and the attacker changes techniques while an attack is underway. The operator also warned that the attacker could be capable of deanonymizing and tracking onion services. The Tor Project has issued no such warning in its release announcements. Related: Firefox Vulnerability Allows Tor User Fingerprinting Related: CryptoBandits Malware Doubles as a Backdoor, Abuses Tor Related: Tor Exit Relays Hijacked
history.summary: Tor 0.4.9.17 was released on November 13 to patch several security issues, including a fix for how relays' built-in DoS protections handle IPv6, in response to an ongoing DDoS attack overwhelming the network with client circuits. The update follows Tor 0.4.9.15, which introduced three DoS protections against a "thunderstorm" of directory requests, but operators report the latest version does not fully shield HSDir relays, as attackers adapt techniques during the attack. Fix: Tor 0.4.9.17 patches security issues and strengthens relay DoS protections against IPv6-based flood attacks.

history.title: Microsoft pushes Windows emergency updates to fix activation failures
history.text: Microsoft has released emergency out-of-band updates to fix Windows activation and licensing failures caused by this month's security updates. As the company confirmed in a Wednesday service alert, this known issue affects organizations that use the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) command-line tool to automate Windows activation and licensing processes. However, Microsoft said that enterprise customers who don't use SLMGR for licensing management and have the KMS client key installed in their image are unaffected. "Devices that are already activated remain activated. Customers whose devices already have the appropriate KMS client key and KMS configuration, and who do not need to run the affected Slmgr.vbs commands, are not expected to be affected," the company noted. On Friday, Microsoft released multiple emergency Windows updates to fix the bug on the following client (Windows 10 21H2/22H2 and Windows 11 23H2) and server (Windows Server 2019/2022/2025) platforms: - Windows Server 2025: KB5136489 - Windows Server 2022: KB5136487 - Windows Server 2019 and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2019: KB5136490 - Windows 11, version 23H2: KB5136483 - Windows 10, version 22H2 ESU and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021: KB5136493 For Windows Server 2025, Windows Server 2022, Windows Server 2019, and Windows 10, the out-of-band updates are available only through the Microsoft Update Catalog. The Windows 11, version 23H2 optional OOB update is available through Windows Update and the Microsoft Update Catalog and can be installed from Settings > Windows Update > Advanced options > Optional updates to download. "This cumulative update includes the improvements from the November 2026 Windows security update," Microsoft added. "For complete guidance and installation instructions, see the relevant KB articles." In January, Microsoft resolved a similar issue that was causing Windows license migration failures during upgrades because impacted devices couldn't register with the Windows Activation server for digital licenses. Last week, it also acknowledged that Windows updates released since the October Patch Tuesday are triggering SQL Server performance and stability issues and that the November 2026 Windows 11 security updates fail to install on systems with the October 2026 preview update. history.summary: Microsoft has released emergency out-of-band updates to fix Windows activation and licensing failures caused by this month's security updates, affecting organizations using the SLMGR tool; the updates target specific Windows 10 and 11 client and Windows Server 2019/2022/2025 platforms and are available via the Microsoft Update Catalog and Windows Update. Systems already activated remain activated, and customers without SLMGR usage and with a KMS client key installed are unaffected. Fix: Emergency updates are available through the Microsoft Update Catalog and Windows Update Advanced options to resolve the activation failures on impacted platforms.

history.title: Amazon Uncovers AI Agent Campaign Targeting LiteLLM, Dify, and Other Apps for API Keys
history.text: Attackers' AI agents have been hunting for weak spots in internet-exposed AI apps such as LiteLLM, One API, and Dify to steal the AI provider keys stored inside, according to the agents' own records. The records, which Amazon's threat intelligence team captured with decoy servers, describe stolen keys being used to run the AI models that powered the search for more keys. The team said this week that it cannot verify the outcomes reported by the agents. It has moderate confidence that the agents ran on ARTEX, an open-source AI tool for penetration testing. The records include a playbook of known entry points for each targeted product. It lists default administrator credentials such as LiteLLM's default master key, unfinished installs that an outsider could take over, and known flaws in Langflow and RAGFlow. In a separate case reported this week, Cloudflare's incident responders saw ARTEX gain access to a compromised API token that had been used for CI/CD. The token had no IP restrictions or rate limiting, and the activity that followed included 400 database dump requests in an hour. The company has not said whether those requests returned any data. An operator gives ARTEX a target and a goal, and a planner agent splits the goal into tasks for worker agents that run security tools. To decide each next step, the agents send their work to a large language model (LLM). The decoy servers, part of a network called MadPot, posed as popular LLM services. From October 3 to late last week, the agents sent it requests that often carried a campaign's full history, including the operators' instructions and the agents' reported findings. Those captured agent records describe work done on systems MadPot does not watch. "Amazon Threat Intelligence did not observe that activity as it happened and cannot verify the outcomes the agents reported, but the records show what the actors were pursuing," the team said. The team assessed, with moderate confidence, that the operators were separate China-linked groups, citing Simplified Chinese prompts and China time zone settings, among other evidence. In the main campaign, the agents looked for internet-exposed AI apps, extracted the provider keys stored inside, verified that the keys worked, and added them to a shared pool. They focused on apps that hold keys for many providers, because one weak admin page there can expose many accounts. Targets named in the records include LLM gateways and proxies such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API and LiteLLM, and AI app builders such as Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat and Ollama. The playbook also covers management and provider settings endpoints that need no login, an authentication bypass through the isCliRequest header in One API family systems, and server-side request forgery (SSRF) through URL-fetch features to reach cloud metadata services. Other entries cover secrets left in client-side JavaScript, source maps, debug routes and environment files. When the agents found cloud credentials, they targeted managed services that host AI models, secret stores, and application identities, prioritizing premium AI models over general cloud access. To find leaked keys, the agents used internet scanning services and certificate transparency logs, and searched GitHub repositories and event archives, npm and PyPI packages, container image layers, notebooks, model-hosting spaces, paste sites, and Telegram channels. The records cover hundreds of targets across AI app platforms and other systems. The team notified AWS customers who may have been affected. Microsoft reported last week that attackers were using agentic AI tools such as ARTEX for GitHub secret hunting, looking for exposed credentials that included API keys for AI inference. On August 26, the company described an earlier RAGFlow attack, in which a hidden hook captured AI provider keys as users entered them, and a compromise of a LiteLLM gateway that exposed provider keys. In its RAGFlow case study, the company had only low confidence about which flaw, if any, let the attackers run code. It did not link those attacks to ARTEX. The decoy records also describe a second campaign in which agents attempted to bypass identity checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges using deepfakes. One verification vendor's server rejected the live deepfake video on every attempt the agents made to record it. The team did not say whether the forged photos of ID documents that the agents also fabricated passed document checks. Over the past eight weeks, Cloudflare's incident responders were called into multiple investigations involving ARTEX and tools built from it. In more than one incident, an attacker gained access to a customer's environment with a major cloud provider and moved directly into the customer's Cloudflare account. The common root cause was static CI/CD tokens that never expired, granting broad access across the customer's cloud setup, according to the company. In the ARTEX case, the compromised token was an account-level API token. The compromise most likely came through a third-party cloud provider, according to the company's incident findings. How the token was first stolen has not been disclosed. New Worker scripts with names such as artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-* and artex-do-* appeared in the account, each name matching a different task. The activity ran at more than 69 requests per minute across several parts of the account. It included attempts to establish persistence and validate session tokens for other third-party apps. Much of this activity was lightly guided by a human operator, the company believes. Whether any attempt at persistence worked has not been disclosed. Over three days this week, more than 50 families of AI penetration testing frameworks tried to scan the company's customers, and the IP addresses seen running such frameworks now number in the thousands. The FBI said in a FLASH alert this week that a range of attackers have used ARTEX since at least August against organizations in many sectors around the world. The alert summarizes 11 earlier reports and describes no new incident. ARTEX's developer made its GitHub repository unavailable on October 8 after reports of abuse, but community forks, archived copies, and a commercial version called ARTEX PRO keep it available. The alert's examples include an earlier campaign against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal information on about 67,000 people, and the ConnectWise compromise. What Defenders Can Check "None of the techniques in these campaigns were new. What AI agents change is the speed and persistence of the attacker," Amazon's threat intelligence team said. The agents succeeded where basic security was missing, including default or hard-coded credentials, keys left in code and public files, interfaces and inference endpoints without authentication, and unpatched software. The team recommends treating AI apps, model gateways, and inference endpoints like other production systems, assuming that exposed secrets will be found quickly, and watching for misuse through unexpected spending or unusual usage. Here is the status of the flaws named in the playbook: Other checks that apply to these attacks: - Change default administrator credentials, such as LiteLLM's default master key, and do not leave a new install unfinished where an outsider could take it over. - Search configuration files, environment variables, deployment scripts, CI/CD pipelines and databases for embedded secrets, keep scanning repositories and container images for exposed ones, and rotate exposed credentials quickly, as the FBI advises. - Give Cloudflare API tokens an expiry date and limit the client IP addresses that can use them. Both are optional token restriction settings, and new tokens carry a cfut_ prefix that secret scanners can detect. - Look for Cloudflare Worker scripts named artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-* or artex-do-*. - Check logs for the 11 IP addresses published with the decoy findings, and for the more than 2,500 addresses that researchers at Cisco Talos link to ARTEX in their indicator files. - The researchers' detection rules for ARTEX are Snort 3 rules 7:76, 7:77 and 7:78, and Snort 2 rules 1:67494, 1:67495 and 1:67496. Rules 7:78 and 1:67496 are off by default and detect traces of norma, the agent harness ARTEX uses.
